transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
The Supreme Court says New Hampshire election officials
are no longer allowed to consider student IDs at all
when verifying voter identity for the midterm elections.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports.
- The Supreme Court ruling means that a student voter
in New Hampshire must continue to show at the polls
a state ID, U.S. passport, or another accepted proof
of their identity that isn't a student ID.
The unsigned order by the high court
is part of an early stage of a legal fight
over one of the latest laws in Republican-led states
that ban registered voters from checking in at the polls
with their student IDs.
There are also lawsuits over Indiana's ban,
as well as a Florida ban that's set to start next year.
Challengers argue these bans violate the U.S. Constitution
by making it harder for eligible students to vote.
Republican state officials claim these bans
support election security, but there is no evidence
of widespread voter fraud involving student IDs.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
- Ohio Governor Mike DeWine says he's a Republican,
and although he says he supports the Republican ticket
as a whole heading into the midterm elections,
he's urging Vivek Ramaswamy, who is vying to succeed DeWine,
to stop running a controversial ad that features
the estranged mother of Democratic opponent Amy Acton.
- The people I've worked with on that ticket
are very, very good people, and look, I'm a Republican,
and so I did my endorsement a few months ago,
but I wanted to talk today about is this ad,
I think, as I said, is deeply, deeply, deeply troubling.
It needs to come down.
- DeWine spoke to reporters about that ad Thursday.
President Trump says Ramaswamy should keep running it.
He talked about it during a Thursday evening's
campaign rally in Iowa.
Earlier in the day, Trump posted on social media
that the ad was, in his words, "hitting pay dirt."
Acton's mother lost custody of Acton and her brother
after their stepfather was indicted
for sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old.
Syrian state media say Israeli forces raided a village
in southwestern Syria, killing a civilian with disabilities.
NPR's Dana Raff reports.
- Syria's state news agency, said Israeli soldiers
entered the village of Jumla in Dara Province
and placed snipers on rooftops.
It said Israeli forces opened fire on a civilian
with disabilities, killing him.
The Israeli military said soldiers in Jumla
fired at a man approaching them.
It said it was reviewing the incident.
The Syrian Arab news agency also said Israeli forces
this week destroyed Farmer's Olive Groves
in Kneitra Province near the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
Israel seized additional territory in southern Syria
after President Bashar al-Assad was toppled
by opposition fighters two years ago,
calling it a security zone.
Dana Raff, NPR News, Amman.
- And you're listening to NPR News.
A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine,
drug makers Moderna and Merck say a vaccine
using mRNA technology,
combined with a standard post-surgery treatment,
cut the risk of melanoma death or recurrence by 42%.
The companies reported the results of a large trial Thursday
and say they are preparing to file for U.S. approval
with an eye toward launching the vaccine in 2027.
Mortgage rates have dipped for the first time
in more than two months,
but NPR's Stephen Basaha reports that rates
are still higher than a year ago,
keeping would-be home buyers on the sidelines.
- Mortgage rates fell this week to 7.32%,
a small dip from last week.
This is for an average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage.
Kate Wood is Nerdwall's housing expert
and says this does not necessarily mean
rates have turned a corner.
- Seeing, okay, this is the first decrease
that we've had after weeks of increases,
like, yes, it's exciting,
but I'd say all the time mortgage rates
do not follow the laws of gravity.
What goes up does not have to come down.
- The fundamentals that have pushed mortgage rates up
have not changed much.
Inflation is still high,
and mortgage rates are still more than a full percentage
point higher than they were a year ago.
Stephen Basaha, NPR News.
- An Emmy-winning actor known for his roles
in Top Gun and Picket Fences has died.
Tom Scarrett was 93.
A statement from Scarrett's family says
he died Wednesday of natural causes.
Scarrett's career spanned decades
from the 1960s to the 2020s, and 1997.
He told a Seattle newspaper that he was once described
as a character actor in a leading man's body.
This is NPR News.
- This message comes from Cure Alzheimer's Fund.
From family to community,
connections and the memories they make are everything.
Cure Alzheimer's Fund empowers scientists
pursuing bold Alzheimer's research.
Learn more at curealz.org.

topics.text: Supreme Court bars New Hampshire officials from accepting student IDs for midterm voter verification
Ohio Governor DeWine urges Vivek Ramaswamy to pull ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother
Syrian state media say Israeli forces killed a disabled civilian in Daraa Province village
Israeli military says it is reviewing shooting of a man approaching its soldiers in Jumla
Israeli forces reportedly destroy olive groves in Quneitra Province near the Golan Heights
Moderna and Merck report mRNA cancer vaccine cuts melanoma death or recurrence risk by 42%
Average 30-year mortgage rate dips to 7.32% for first time in over two months
Emmy-winning actor Tom Skerritt, known for Top Gun and Picket Fences, dies at 93
